Sometimes, but not cleanly. Like, if I really notice it and kind of yank myself back mentally, I can stop after a second, but it doesn’t feel like just deciding to stop a normal habit. It’s more like I’m stuck in the wrong gear.

I don’t think there’s a specific thought like that, no. Not like, “If I don’t tap, something bad will happen,” or “I have to pause or else…” I’ve tried to look for that, because I know that’s probably what you’re asking, whether there’s some fear behind it, but I can’t really find one.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I don’t think I can honestly say I believe that, no. Not in the sense of, like, some outside force grabbing me or making my body stop or move. I haven’t had a clear thought like, “Something else is moving my arms,” or “Something is freezing me on purpose.”

It’s more that when it happens, I feel stuck and confused, and afterward I try to make sense of it. In the moment it can feel like my body just isn’t following through the way it should, but I don’t know that I would call that an outside force. I’m careful with that because I don’t want to say yes and make it sound like I’m certain about something I’m not certain about.

So… no, I don’t really believe there’s a force controlling my body. I just know that sometimes I stop moving or get caught in a motion, and I can’t explain why very well.

From the dialogue so far and your candidates from the previous turn, list the disorders this patient could have.\n\n[Current Turn]\n15\n\n[Previous Candidates]\nF20.2, F06.1, F44.4\n\n[Dialogue History]\nDoctor: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?\n\nPatient: Yeah… um, I came in because things have been getting strange at work, mostly at the register. I’m a cashier, and I keep sort of… getting stuck doing things that don’t really match what’s happening. Like a customer will be standing there waiting to pay, and instead of just scanning the next thing or opening the drawer, I’ll start tapping the scanner in a pattern. Not hard, just like… tap-tap, pause, tap, and then I’ll do it again like I need to finish it the right way.\n\nAnd sometimes I freeze with my hand just over the cash drawer, like I know I’m supposed to move, I know the customer is right there watching me, but my hand just stays there for a bit. It feels embarrassing because I can tell it doesn’t look normal, and it slows everything down. Last week it happened enough that my supervisor wrote me up, and that’s what made me think I probably needed to come talk to someone instead of just telling myself I’m tired or distracted.\n\nDoctor: When you do the tapping pattern, does it feel like you have to do it until it feels just right?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if it’s exactly “just right,” like… I’m not thinking, “Okay, three taps and then it’s safe” or anything that clear. It’s more like I get stuck in it. I’ll be at the register, and the customer is standing there, and instead of doing the normal next step, I start tapping the scanner in this little pattern, and it feels like I can’t just break out of it right away.\n\nSometimes it’s the tapping, sometimes I just freeze with my hand over the cash drawer, like my arm forgot what it was supposed to do even though I know perfectly well I’m supposed to keep moving. And then I’m aware they’re waiting, and that makes it worse because I’m thinking, “Come on, just open the drawer,” but I’m still just… paused there.\n\nIt’s embarrassing. It happened enough last week that my supervisor wrote me up, so it’s not just me being picky or fussy about how I do things. It’s more like I get caught doing something that doesn’t fit the moment, and I can’t smoothly get back to the transaction.\n\nDoctor: Right before the tapping or freezing starts, do you feel a build-up of tension or an urge in your body that gets relieved when it happens?\n\nPatient: Not really in the way you’re describing, I don’t think. I’m not aware of, like, a pressure building up in my chest or my hands or something, and then the tapping makes it go away. It’s more that I’m just at the register, doing the transaction, and then I sort of get caught in something that doesn’t fit what’s happening.\n\nLike I’ll have the scanner right there and instead of moving on to the next item or finishing with the customer, I’ll tap it in that little pattern, or my hand will just hover over the cash drawer when I’m supposed to open it. Last week it slowed me down and my supervisor wrote me up for it, so now I’m kind of nervous every time I’m at the register.\n\nDoctor: When the tapping or freezing starts, can you stop it if you force yourself to?\n\nPatient: Sometimes, but not cleanly. Like, if I really notice it and kind of yank myself back mentally, I can stop after a second, but it doesn’t feel like just deciding to stop a normal habit. It’s more like I’m stuck in the wrong gear.\n\nAt the register, I’ll know exactly what I’m supposed to be doing — the customer’s waiting, the items are there, the drawer needs to open — and then my hand is tapping the scanner, or it’s just hovering over the cash drawer. I’ll think, “Stop doing that, move,” and there’s this awkward delay before I actually do. So I can force myself sometimes, yes, but it takes effort, and by then the moment has already gotten strange and the customer is looking at me.\n\nThat’s part of why it got bad enough at work. It wasn’t just in my head. It slowed the line down, and last week my supervisor wrote me up for it.\n\nDoctor: When this happens, do you have an unwanted thought or fear in your mind that makes you feel you need to tap or pause?\n\nPatient: I don’t think there’s a specific thought like that, no. Not like, “If I don’t tap, something bad will happen,” or “I have to pause or else…” I’ve tried to look for that, because I know that’s probably what you’re asking, whether there’s some fear behind it, but I can’t really find one.\n\nIt’s more confusing than that. I’ll be in the middle of the transaction, and then suddenly I’m tapping or paused, and only after a second do I realize, “Why am I doing this? The person is waiting.” There isn’t a clear unwanted thought that comes first, at least not one I can catch. It’s not like I’m afraid the register will be wrong or the customer will get hurt or anything specific like that.\n\nMostly what comes into my mind is after it starts — embarrassment, and this kind of frustrated feeling, like, “Move already, just finish the sale.” But that’s more because I’m stuck, not what makes me do it in the first place. So… no, I haven’t noticed a fear or thought that tells me I need to tap or pause.\n\nDoctor: Outside of these episodes at the register, do you ever have sudden movements or sounds you make over and over, even when you’re not trying to?\n\nPatient: I don’t think so… not that I’ve noticed in a regular way. I mean, everybody makes little noises sometimes or shifts around, but I don’t have, like, a repeated sound I keep making without meaning to, at least not that anyone has pointed out to me.\n\nThe tapping thing is really mostly what I’ve been aware of, and especially because it happens when I’m supposed to be doing something specific at the register. Outside of that, I can’t really say there’s some sudden movement or noise that keeps happening over and over. If it is happening, I’m not aware of it the same way.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices that other people can’t hear?\n\nPatient: Yes… I mean, I guess yes. I don’t always like saying it that way, because it sounds… I don’t know, it sounds like I’m making it more dramatic than it is. But most days I hear what sounds like a couple people talking nearby, like just off to the side of me.\n\nAt work it’s especially noticeable. I’ll be at the register or near the front, and I’ll hear someone say my name from the stockroom, or I’ll hear a voice say something like I rang something up wrong. Not shouting, usually — more like people talking close enough that I should be able to turn and see them. So I do turn around, or I look toward the stockroom, and there’s nobody there. Or I’ll ask, “Did someone call me?” and people look at me like, no, they didn’t hear anything.\n\nIt’s not every single minute, but it’s often enough that I’ve started second-guessing myself. Like if I hear my name, I don’t immediately answer anymore because sometimes there isn’t anyone. It’s embarrassing, honestly. It makes me feel like I can’t trust my own ears.\n\nDoctor: Have you started using any drugs or medicines recently?\n\nPatient: Um… I don’t think so. Not that I’d call “started,” anyway.\n\nI’m trying to think if there’s anything new, because sometimes you don’t realize what counts. Like, do you mean prescription medicine, or like cold medicine, or something someone gives you? I haven’t started anything that stands out in my mind recently. I’m not using drugs, if that’s what you mean.\n\nI mean, I can go home and look if you want me to be exact, because I’m not always great at remembering every little thing, but there hasn’t been some new pill or drug where I’d say, “Oh yes, that began right before this.” Nothing like that that I can point to.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any recent seizure, head injury, or other neurological illness?\n\nPatient: Not that I can think of, no. I mean, I haven’t had a seizure that I know of, and I don’t remember hitting my head recently or having some kind of medical thing like that happen.\n\nI’m trying to be careful because if you ask me something very specific, I start wondering if I’m forgetting something small, like bumping my head on a cabinet or getting dizzy once or something, but nothing major comes to mind. No accident, no fall where I blacked out, no doctor telling me I had a neurological illness. So… as far as I know, no.\n\nDoctor: When you freeze, if someone gently tries to move your arm, does it stay in the new position they put it in?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure about that exact thing — like, nobody’s really taken my arm and tested it that way, putting it somewhere and seeing if it stays. At least not that I remember.\n\nWhat happens more is I sort of get stuck in the middle of something. Like at the register, I’ll have my hand over the cash drawer, and I know there’s a customer right there waiting, and I’m supposed to just take the money or give change, but I freeze for a bit. Or I’ll start tapping the scanner in this pattern, and it doesn’t really fit what I’m supposed to be doing at that moment. It’s embarrassing because it looks like I’m fooling around or not paying attention, but it doesn’t feel like that from the inside.\n\nThat’s actually part of why I came in. Last week I got written up at work over it, because I was doing those things at the register — getting stuck, tapping, not moving on when I should — and it held things up. But as far as someone moving my arm and it staying there, I don’t know. I haven’t noticed that specifically.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone ever moved one of your arms or hands during one of these freezes and then it stayed in that new position for a while?\n\nPatient: I don’t think anyone has actually done that, no — not like moved my arm and then checked whether it stayed there. I don’t remember anybody repositioning my hand during one of those moments.\n\nWhat I can say is, the reason I came in is more that at the register I keep getting stuck doing things that don’t fit what’s happening. Like I’ll have my hand just hovering over the cash drawer while the customer is standing there waiting, and I know I’m supposed to move, but I just… don’t, for a bit. Or I start tapping the scanner in a pattern, and it’s not useful, it’s not part of ringing them up, it’s just this thing I’m doing.\n\nAnd last week that got me written up, because it held things up and looked bad, like I was messing around or ignoring the line. So that’s the kind of freezing I mean. But the arm-staying-where-someone-put-it thing, I honestly don’t know.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel like someone or something is controlling your actions or putting thoughts into your mind?\n\nPatient: I don’t know that I’d put it that way, exactly. Like… “controlling my actions” sounds very dramatic, like a puppet or something, and I’m not sure that’s what I mean. I do have times where I feel like I’m not fully the one deciding what I’m doing in the moment, but I also worry I’m describing it wrong.\n\nAnd with thoughts being put in my mind… I’m not sure. I have thoughts that feel intrusive or like they come out of nowhere, but I don’t know if that means someone is putting them there. I haven’t really caught myself thinking, “This specific person is inserting thoughts into my head,” if that’s what you mean.\n\nIt’s more confusing than that. Sometimes I’m doing something and it feels like my brain is not cooperating, or like there’s a delay between me knowing what I should do and actually doing it. But I don’t know if that counts as being controlled. I don’t want to say yes to something if I’m just misunderstanding the question.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe an outside force is making your body move or stop moving?\n\nPatient: I don’t think I can honestly say I believe that, no. Not in the sense of, like, some outside force grabbing me or making my body stop or move. I haven’t had a clear thought like, “Something else is moving my arms,” or “Something is freezing me on purpose.”\n\nIt’s more that when it happens, I feel stuck and confused, and afterward I try to make sense of it. In the moment it can feel like my body just isn’t following through the way it should, but I don’t know that I would call that an outside force. I’m careful with that because I don’t want to say yes and make it sound like I’m certain about something I’m not certain about.\n\nSo… no, I don’t really believe there’s a force controlling my body. I just know that sometimes I stop moving or get caught in a motion, and I can’t explain why very well.\n\nDoctor: Do the freezing or tapping episodes happen when you’re alone, or only when other people are around?\n\nPatient: It’s mostly when I’m at the register, when people are around and there’s that pressure of the customer waiting and the line behind them. That’s where I notice it the most, because it becomes obvious right away — like my hand will be over the cash drawer and I know I’m supposed to take the change out or close it or do the next step, and instead I just sort of hold there too long.\n\nThe tapping, too, that’s been happening there. I’ll tap the scanner in this little pattern, and it’s not part of the job, it doesn’t help anything, but I’ll catch myself doing it while someone is standing there waiting. So I can’t say it only happens with people around in some grand sense, because I’m not watching myself every minute when I’m alone, but the episodes that are causing trouble are definitely at work, in front of customers.\n\nThat’s why I came in, really. It got to where it wasn’t just me feeling strange about it — last week I got written up because it slowed things down and looked like I was fooling around or not paying attention. So… the ones I’m sure about are when other people are there, especially at the register.\n\nDoctor: When you freeze or start tapping, do you also feel confused about what is happening around you?\n\nPatient: Yes… I mean, confused, but maybe not in the way people might mean, like I don’t lose track of where I am or anything. I know I’m at the register, I know there’s a customer there, I know I’m supposed to be doing the next part of the transaction. But then I get stuck doing something that doesn’t fit the moment.\n\nLike with the scanner tapping — I’ll start tapping it in this little pattern, and part of me knows, “This isn’t what I’m supposed to be doing right now,” because the customer is standing there waiting. Or I’ll have my hand over the cash drawer and I’m supposed to take the change out or close the drawer, and I just freeze there for too long. So the confusion is more like… why am I doing this, why can’t I just move on to the next step like normal?\n\nThat’s actually why I came in. It’s not just embarrassing anymore. Last week I got written up because it slowed things down and looked like I was messing around or not paying attention, but I wasn’t trying to be difficult. I was just stuck in it, and it didn’t match what was happening around me.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. Not exactly like that, no… or at least I’m not sure I’d describe it as them having a whole conversation about me, like two people sitting there discussing me in detail.

What happens more is that most days I hear what sounds like a couple of people off to the side of me, like nearby but not right in front of me. So… I don’t know if that counts as them talking to each other about me. It’s more like voices or people nearby commenting or calling to me, not usually a full back-and-forth conversation where they’re saying “he” or “him” and discussing me.

Last week I got written up because I kept slowing the line down, and to them it looked like I was fooling around or not paying attention. I wasn’t trying to. I just couldn’t move smoothly to the next step, even when people were right there waiting.\n\nDoctor: When someone lightly guides your arm during one of these freezes, does your arm go along automatically even if you weren’t trying to move it?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure about the arm being guided, honestly. I don’t think anyone has really taken my arm and moved it during one of those moments, at least not that I remember. At work people usually just say my name or look annoyed, they don’t physically guide me.\n\nWhat I can say is, when it happens, it’s like I’m stuck doing something that doesn’t match what I’m supposed to be doing. Like I’ll be at the register and instead of just scanning the item or moving to the cash drawer, I’ll tap the scanner in this little pattern, or I’ll freeze with my hand over the drawer while the customer is standing there waiting. It’s embarrassing because I know the next step should be simple, but I don’t move into it right away.\n\nThat’s really why I came in, because it’s started affecting the job. Last week I got written up for it, because from the outside it probably looks like I’m messing around or not paying attention, but I’m not trying to do it. I just sort of get caught there. As far as someone guiding my arm and it going along automatically, I don’t know — I haven’t noticed that specifically.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself talking much less than usual lately?\n\nPatient: Yeah… I think so. My wife has pointed that out, actually. She’ll ask me what’s wrong, or if I’m upset with her, and I’m not really upset. I still care about her and the kids, I really do. It’s not like I stopped loving them or anything like that. It’s more like… the words don’t come up, or I don’t have the energy to explain anything, so I just kind of shrug or say, “I don’t know.”\n\nAnd I’ve noticed it with my son too. He’s away at college, and I used to call him more, or at least think, “I should check in, see how his classes are going.” Now I’ll think about calling, and then I just don’t. Not because I don’t want to know, exactly, but there’s no push behind it. Like the thought is there, but it doesn’t turn into doing it.\n\nSame with other things. I used to meet up with this kayak group sometimes, and I’ve stopped going. I’ve got little repair projects at home too — things I normally would’ve tinkered with, fixed, organized — and they just sit there. If someone asks me why I haven’t done them, I don’t have a good answer. I just don’t seem to have much to say."
